ABSTRACT
Nanocellulose has gained much attention because of its excellent properties. Cationic cellulose nanocrystals
(cCNC) shows good adsorptivity toward negative ions and molecules. Phosphate binders are most used to treat
hyperphosphatemia and it is significant to develop its alternatives with high specific and low cost in the clinic.
Herein, we prepared cCNC and characterized it by FTIR, TEM, dynamic light scattering, and viscosity method.
We simulated the binding process of cationic cellulose for phosphate and used it as phosphate binder for
hyperphosphatemia therapy to study the phosphate binding effect and evaluate the oral toxicity. Cationic cel -
lulose improved the conditions of mice models and efficiently decreased the level of phosphate in the serum.
cCNC had a better binding effect than cationic microcrystalline cellulose both in vitro and in vivo . cCNC could be
used as alternatives to phosphate binder for therapy of chronic renal failure and hyperphosphatemia.
1. Introduction
Cellulose, which is a kind of renewable natural polymer material
with wide sources, has a large specific surface area and a network
structure in space ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2018 ). Nanocellulose
mainly includes cellulose nanocrystals (CNC), cellulose nanofibrils, and
bacterial cellulose, which has gained much attention because of its
remarkable physical properties, special surface chemistry, and excellent
biological properties ( Du et al., 2019 ; Li, Cha, Mou et al., 2018 ; Liu, Li
et al., 2016 ; Liu, Cheng et al., 2016 ; Xu et al., 2018 ; Zhang, Zeng, Xie, Li,
& Li, 2016 ). Nanocrystalline cellulose is usually prepared by hydrolysis
of plant fibers with sulfuric acid ( Liu, Li et al., 2016 ; Liu, Cheng et al.,
2016 ), which has a diameter of 10~20 nm and a length of 100~600 nm
( Tang, Zhang, Zhao, Guo, & Zhang, 2018 ; Wang & Cha, 2019 ).
Cellulose can be modified by grafting functional groups due to the
abundant hydroxyl groups in molecular chains ( Cha, He, & Ni, 2012 ).
Cationic cellulose has a larger surface charge density than un-modified
cellulose ( Huang et al., 2018 ). Cationic microcrystalline cellulose
(cMCC) and cationic cellulose nanocrystals (cCNC) were well dispersed
and stable in aqueous media due to enhanced cationic surface charge
density ( Zaman, Xiao, Chibante, & Ni, 2012 ). cMCC and cCNC can bind
anionic ions (such as phosphate ion) and show high biosafety and
biocompatibility ( Li et al., 2019 ), which exhibit broad application
prospects in food and medical industries as additives.
Chronic renal failure (CRF) is one of the chronic kidney diseases,
which threatens health all over the world ( Walser, 1973 ; Zhang, Vaziri

et al., 2016 ). Accumulation of phosphorus in plasma is typical in CRF
patients due to the reduced ability of the kidneys to remove phosphorus
from circulating plasma ( Tohno et al., 1999 ; Yaguchi, Tatemichi,
Takeda, & Kobayashi, 2017 ). Excess phosphorus in plasma will induce
hyperphosphatemia, which is a widely recognized risk factor for mor -
tality and cardiovascular disease ( Cozzolino, Ciceri, & Galassi, 2019 ).
Meanwhile, fiscal expenditure on hyperphosphatemia is increasing
yearly. It is essential to cure hyperphosphatemia effectively.
Therapy of hyperphosphatemia in patients with CRF mainly contains
dialysis and orally administering phosphate binders in the clinic ( Patel,
Bernard, & Elder, 2016 ; Shaman & Kowalski, 2016 ). Dialysis can replace
part of the kidney metabolism, which may slightly reduce the phos -
phorus level. Phosphate binders are always used as adjuvant medicine
for reducing phosphorus level ( Brunner-Ziegler, Froschl, Hiebinger, &
Zsifkovits, 2011 ), which can bind compounds containing P in the in -
testines and removed them through feces.
The most used phosphate binders, including calcium carbonate,
aluminum hydroxide, lanthanum carbonate, and Sevelamer, always
possess severe deficiencies and side effects ( Lo et al., 2008 ; Sprague,
2007 ; Sturtevant et al., 2004 ). Calcium carbonate and aluminum hy -
droxide, which increase calcium and aluminum in plasma of patients,
would further aggravate the burden of kidney ( de Francisco et al., 2010 ).
Lanthanum carbonate, an effective and well-tolerated phosphate binder
for reducing phosphate levels in patients, increases the financial burden
due to its high cost ( Behets, Verberckmoes, D ’ Haese, & De Broe, 2004 ).
Sevelamer, a cationic synthetic polymer, could induce gastrointestinal
diseases and reduce absorption of fat and vitamin in patients ( Zhou, Li,
Xie, & Lin, 2018 ). It is essential to develop a new kind of phosphate
binders with high efficiency and low cost, which would benefit the
therapy of CRF in the clinic.
Herein, we prepared cCNC and studied the binding process of cCNC
for phosphate. We characterized the surface morphology, zeta potential,
and degree of polymerization (DP) of cMCC and cCNC. We simulated the
binding process of cMCC and cCNC for phosphate and used them as
phosphate binders for therapy of hyperphosphatemia in mice with CRF
( Fig. 1 ). We built mice models with CRF and hyperphosphatemia by
administering the mice with adenine suspension. We studied the effect
of cMCC and cCNC on mice models with CRF and hyperphosphatemia by
gavage of phosphate binders for two weeks. We measured the levels of P,
Ca, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine (CREA) in serum, and
detected the content of P in feces. We evaluated the toxicity of cMCC and
cCNC through observing pathology of kidney and small intestines. Our
work studied cCNC as a phosphate binder, which would benefit the
therapy of CRF in the clinic.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
We bought cMCC from WengJiang Regent (Shaoguan, China), whose
degree of substitution (DS) [substituent group: (2, 3-epoxypropyl)trime -
thylammonium chloride (EPTAC) group] was 0.03, 0.06, 0.09, 0.12, and

0.15. We bought adenine from Aladdin (Shanghai, China). We obtained
softwood bleached kraft pulp (SWBK) from Celgar Pulp Company,
Canada. All the other reagents were analytical grade and used as
received.
We bought BALB/c male mice (specific pathogen free, six weeks)
from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd. All
experiments were subjected to review and approval of the Animal Care
and Use Committee of National Center for Nanoscience and Technology
(approval number: 2019-wangmz-02).
2.2. Preparation of CNC and cCNC
We prepared CNC from SWBK by sulfuric acid hydrolysis as
described previously ( Wang et al., 2012 ). We mixed SWBK with sulfuric
acid (60 %) in reaction kettle. The ratio of sulfuric acid to SWBK was 7 : 1
( v / w ). After reaction at 40
◦
C for 4 h, we added 10-fold deionized water
to quench the hydrolysis. We dialyzed the dispersion until the pH of the
dialysis water no longer changed. We centrifuged the dispersion at
9056 g for 10 min and then freeze-dried to obtain CNC.
We prepared cCNC as described by previous work ( Zaman et al.,
2012 ). We mixed 1000 mg of CNC and 50 mg of sodium hydroxide
thoroughly for 5 min at room temperature and they were left to cool to
room temperature. We transferred the solid mixture to a polyethylene
bag followed by addition of water and added the cationization agent
(EPTAC) dropwise. Then the reaction mixture was kept in a thermo -
stated ultrasonic water bath at 65
◦
C for 4 h. After that, the product was
precipitated in 95 % ethanol, purified, and concentrated to obtain cCNC.

We mounted cMCC on a specimen holder using conductive adhesion.
We used an ion sputtering instrument (Model ACS-4000-C4, Ulvac,
Japan) to sputter cMCC for 30 s. We observed the morphology of cMCC
by scanning electron microscope (SEM, S4800, Hitachi, Japan) at an

We dripped cCNC dispersion (10 μ L, 0.05 % w / w ) on a copper grid.
After room temperature drying, we stained cCNC using uranyl acetate
for 2 min. We observed the morphology of cCNC by transmission elec -
tron microscope (TEM, HT7700, Hitachi, Japan) at an acceleration
voltage of 120 kV.

2.5. Establishment of mice models with CRF and hyperphosphatemia
We built mice models with CRF and hyperphosphatemia by admin -
istration of adenine suspension ( Long et al., 2019 ). Briefly, we admin -
istered the mice with 200 μ L of adenine suspension (20 mg/mL) by
gavage once every other day, and the mice with water in control group.
We observed the conditions of the mice in the experiment every day and
stopped administration after ten days. After executing the mice in model
and control groups, we observed the pathology of kidneys in mice and
measured the levels of P, Ca, BUN, and CREA in serum.
2.6. Therapy of hyperphosphatemia in mice
We divided the mice models with CRF and hyperphosphatemia into
three groups, including cMCC group, cCNC group, and negative control
group. We administered the mice in cMCC group with 200 μ L of cMCC
dispersion (0.6 %) and the mice in cCNC group with 200 μ L of cCNC
dispersion (0.6 %) by gavage once a day. And we administered the mice
in negative control group with an equal volume of normal saline. The
mice without treatment were normal control. We collected the feces,
blood, kidneys, livers, and small intestines of mice after they were
sacrificed by CO
2
asphyxiation.

We centrifuged the blood at 3000 rpm for 10 min to obtain serum.
We measured the levels of P, Ca, BUN, CREA, alanine aminotransferase
(ALT), glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (AST), total cholesterol (TC),

3. Results and discussion

We tested the DP of cationic cellulose ( Fig. 2 c). With the increase of
DS, the DP of cMCC and cCNC almost kept stable. DS could hardly affect
the DP of cationic cellulose.
We observed the surface morphology of cationic cellulose ( Fig. 2 d).
cMCC was a spherical particle, while cCNC was a rigid rod-like nano -
particle. We counted the size of the particles through their micrographs.
cMCC had a diameter of about 15 μ m, while cCNC had a diameter of
about 10 nm and a length of about 150 nm. cCNC had a larger specific
surface area than cMCC since the specific surface area of cCNC was 1067
times that of cMCC.
We studied the stability of cCNC in different pH condition. The mixed
dispersion was homogeneous with no precipitation after the cCNC was
mixed with buffer solutions. cCNC was stable in simulated gastric pH
condition and intestinal pH condition.
3.2. Binding efficiency of phosphate on cationic cellulose
We studied the effect of DS and concentration on binding efficiency
of phosphate on cationic cellulose ( Fig. 3 ). cMCC and cCNC can adsorb
phosphate ions due to their cationic surface. The binding efficiency is
affected by various factors including time, temperature, pH value,
concentration of phosphate ion, concentration, and DS of cMCC or cCNC
( Arai & Sparks, 2001 ).
With the increase of DS or concentration of cMCC and cCNC, the
binding efficiency of phosphate increased rapidly and then almost kept
stable. When the DS was 0.09, the binding efficiency of phosphate was
76.5 % and 89.2 % for cMCC and cCNC ( Fig. 3 a). When the concen -
tration was 0.6 wt%, the binding efficiency of phosphate was 78.6 % and
92.5 % for cMCC and cCNC, respectively ( Fig. 3 b).
The binding efficiency of cCNC was better than that of cMCC since
the larger specific surface area of cCNC. The adsorption behaviors were
mainly ascribed to both physic-sorption and chemic-sorption. The ab -
sorption mechanism could be interpreted as the electrostatic attraction
and ion exchange reaction between cationic cellulose and phosphate
ions ( Liu & Zhang, 2015 ). In the first stage, as the degree of substitution
or concentration increased, the number of charges increased and the
contact probability between cCNC and phosphate increased ( Zhang, Li,
& Liu, 2015 ). Thus, the binding efficiency of phosphate increased
rapidly. In the second stage, steric hindrance occurred due to the
adsorption of a large amount of phosphate. Therefore, the binding ef -
ficiency of phosphate almost kept stable.

We compared cCNC with these commonly used phosphorus binders.
The binding capacity of cCNC was 74.3 mg/g, while that of calcium
carbonate and Sevelamer carbonate was about 39 mg/g and 21 mg/g,
respectively ( Gutekunst, 2016 ). The phosphate-binding efficiency of
cCNC was higher than that of these commonly used phosphorus binders.
We used 0.6 wt% of cMCC and cCNC suspension whose DS was 0.09
for therapy of hyperphosphatemia in mice.
3.3. Evaluation of mice models with CRF and hyperphosphatemia
We measured the levels of P, Ca, BUN, and CREA in serum and
observed the pathology of kidneys to evaluate the mice models with CRF
and hyperphosphatemia.
High contents of P and Ca were found in patients due to decreased
capacity of kidneys for reducing P and Ca, which might induce
hyperphosphatemia. The contents of P and Ca in mice treated with
adenine were about 10 % and 50 % higher than those of mice in control
group ( Fig. 4 a).
BUN and CREA increased by times in patients with CRF because the
destroyed kidney cannot remove these metabolites normally ( Kim, Lhee,
& Lee, 2006 ). The levels of BUN and CREA in mice treated with adenine
increased by at least two times more than that of mice in control group
( Fig. 4 b), revealing that the mice treated with adenine suffered from
renal insufficiency.
The serious changes will happen in the kidneys of patients with CRF,
such as glomerular swelling ( Chen, Wang, & Lang, 2016 ). In normal
mice, cells in the glomerulus arranged neatly, and collecting duct in
renal medulla distributed uniformly. After treating with adenine for ten
days, the renal fibrosis appeared in model mice. Compared with the
normal mice, inflammatory infiltration, the vacuolar degeneration in

The above results confirmed that the mice were infected with CRF

3.4. Therapy of mice with CRF and hyperphosphatemia
We studied the curative effect of cMCC and cCNC on model mice
with CRF and hyperphosphatemia by measuring the contents of P, Ca,
BUN, and CREA in serum of mice after they were treated with cationic
cellulose.
The contents of P in serum of model mice kept high level within two
weeks, and that of mice decreased sharply and were almost equal to the
normal mice after treating with cationic cellulose ( Fig. 5 a). The contents
of P in serum of mice treated with cCNC were 18.8 % lower than that of
mice treated with cMCC.

cationic cellulose on trace elements in mice. Phosphate binders used in
the clinic may affect the metabolism of trace elements in serum, espe -
cially Ca ( Veighey, Booth, & Davenport, 2011 ). Cationic cellulose would
not affect the trace elements in serum of mice because the contents of Ca
always keep at a stable level ( Fig. 5 b), which prohibited the side effect of
phosphate binders.
The contents of BUN and CREA in serum almost kept stable within
two weeks ( Fig. 5 c and d). Compared with the model mice, inflamma -
tory infiltration was improved in mice treated with cationic cellulose
( Fig. 5 e). The mice treated with cCNC had better conditions in the
kidney than those treated with cMCC.
We supposed that the cationic cellulose would benefit hyper -
phosphatemia therapy in mice with CRF because they could bind
phosphate in intestines, so we measured the content of P in feces. The
model mice (19.4 μ mol/L) showed no significant difference to the con -
trol mice (18.4 μ mol/L). The content of P in feces increased by 36.9 %
and 52.7 % after treatment by cMCC and cCNC ( Fig. 6 a), which resulted
in the content of P in serum of mice decreased, illustrating that cationic
cellulose treated the mice with CRF and hyperphosphatemia by binding
phosphate in intestines.
Serum P is a kind of anionic compounds that contain P, which is
mainly obtained from food and exists in the form of organic or inorganic
compounds in the blood. cCNC and cMCC, which are polymers with

cationic ions, acted as an adsorbent for anionic compounds in intestines
(Fig. 6b). They bond compounds containing P in the intestines and
removed them effectively through feces. cCNC had a better binding ef -
fect than cMCC.
3.5. Liver function of mice
Long-term administration of phosphate binders would induce hepa -
totoxicity, so it was essential for us to qualitatively evaluate the hepa -
totoxicity of cationic cellulose after oral administration (Pepper,
Campbell, Yaqoob, Roberts, & Fan, 2011). The levels of ALT and AST
increased when hepatotoxicity happened, and necrosis would appear in
the hepatocytes (Li, Cha, Zhang et al., 2018). Cationic cellulose showed
no influence on the levels of ALT and AST in serum of mice (Fig. 7a and
b), revealing that the cMCC and cCNC would not increase the levels of
hepatic biomarkers. Hepatocytes were in normal range and morphology
in all groups (Fig. 7c), illustrating that cationic cellulose showed no side
effect on hepatic tissues. cMCC and cCNC showed almost no hepato -
toxicity after administration for 2 weeks.
3.6. Blood lipid of mice
Phosphate binders could affect the level of blood lipids after long-
term administration (Neradova et al., 2017). We detected the content
of blood lipids, including TC, TG, HDLC, and LDLC. The level of TC of
mice administered with cationic cellulose increased slightly (Fig. 8a),
which showed no difference to that of control mice and model mice. The
level of TG in model mice was 15 % less than that in control mice, and
the level of TG in model mice increased after administration of cationic
cellulose (Fig. 8b). Cationic cellulose showed no effect on the levels of
HDLC and LDLC since they kept stable in all groups (Fig. 8c and d).
Cationic cellulose regulated the level of TG in model mice and improved
the living conditions of them.
3.7. Pathology of small intestines of mice
Small intestine is responsible for the absorption of nutrients and
minerals from food, where most chemical digestion takes place, and it
supports the immune system (Fields et al., 1986). We studied the effect
of long-term administration of cationic cellulose on small intestines by
observing the morphology of small intestines (Fig. 9). Intestinal villi
were finger-like projections, and each villus was stretching. There was
nearly no difference with each other among these four groups, so
cationic cellulose had no effect on intestines.
4. Conclusions
We successfully prepared cCNC by grafting EPTAC onto the CNC
surface. And we simulated the binding process of phosphate on cationic
cellulose. Then, we studied the effect of them on mice models with CRF
and hyperphosphatemia. Compared with phosphate binders used in the
clinic, cationic cellulose treated hyperphosphatemia effectively without
affecting the metabolism of trace elements. Cationic cellulose treated
hyperphosphatemia by binding phosphate in intestines. cMCC and cCNC
can effectively decrease the levels of P in serum, remove P through feces,
and improve the condition of kidney in model mice. cCNC had a better
binding effect than cMCC both in vitro and in vivo. After a long-term
administration, cationic cellulose was harmless to liver and intestines
and restored the level of TG in serum of mice. cCNC could be used as
alternatives to phosphate binder and had good potential in therapy of
CRF and hyperphosphatemia.
